podcast.body: Following its release, rumors spread that The Kingsmen intentionally garbled the lyrics to conceal sexually explicit content about a Jamaican sailor. Though no one knew for sure, the alleged "secret lyrics" circulated among teenagers, prompting one to contact the governor of Indiana, who subsequently banned the song. This controversy paradoxically boosted the song's mystique and national chart performance. The publishing company offered $1,000 to anyone proving the lyrics were obscene, and the FBI launched a two-year investigation, analyzing the recording forwards and backwards, concluding that the lyrics were "unintelligible at any speed." "Rumors began to spread that the Kingsman had intentionally garbled the lyrics to cover up what was actually being sung."

podcast.body: Larry Page pointed to this song by The Kingsmen as an inspiration for Ray Davis. Page advised Ray that since he wasn't a great singer, the group should "concentrate on riffs," and encouraged him to create something similar to "Louie Louie," which had recently been released in the UK on Pye Records, the same label as The Kinks. "In particular, he'd pointed Ray to Louis Louis by the Kingsman, which had recently been released in the UK on Pye... and told him to do something like that."

podcast.body: The Kingsmen's notoriously amateurish version of "Louie Louie" was recorded in late fall 1963 at Northwest Recorders in Portland, after Jack Ely's voice was strained from a 90-minute live performance of the song the previous night. The recording features Ely's slurred vocals due to a high microphone and braces, drummer Lynn Easton's accidental drumstick click and yelled obscenity, and Ely's mistimed re-entry after the solo. Initially rejected by Capitol Records, it gained national traction after a Boston DJ played it as "worst record of the week," sparking immense public demand and leading to a number 2 chart position. "The Kingsmen did their best to copy the rock and rock in Robert's version, right down to his shout of let's give it to them right now, but it was shockingly amateurish."

podcast.body: The influence of the "three-cord trick" pattern, notably from Chuck Berry's "Havana Moon," played a significant role in the foundational chord sequences of this song, making it one of the most important in rock music. "And between that and the influence of Havana Moon on records like Louis Louis and Wild Thing, the three-cord trick became one of the most important chord sequences in rock music."

podcast.body: The most famous version of this song was a 1963 recording by The Kingsmen, a garage band. It was done in one take using a single overhead microphone, and lead singer Lynn Easton, wearing heavy braces, had to bend his neck back to sing into the mic, resulting in unintelligible lyrics. "The most famous version is a 1963 recording by a garage man called the Kingsman."

The FBI conducted a six-month sound analysis test but could not prove the pornographic nature of the lyrics. "The Kingsman and Louis Louis recorded their slot-proc anthem for 50 bucks."

podcast.body: This track, considered an all-time classic and one of the most famous Garage Rock anthems, was recorded on April 6, 1963, in Portland, Oregon. It cost only $50 to produce and was a cover of an obscure 1957 R&B song by Louisiana singer Richard Berry. The session took place at Northwestern Motion Pictures and Recording, produced by a local DJ. The band blasted it out in a single take, meaning the released version is their only studio performance that day. The arrangement changed the original beat, and singer Joe Eli, wearing heavy braces, sang directly into a single boom microphone, contributing to the unintelligible vocals. The song is famous for a mistake: after the guitar solo, Eli comes in early, stops, and drummer Lynn Easton plays an extra drum fill to cover the error; this mistake is now intentionally replicated in modern performances. It became a regional, then national, hit, and rumors of pornographic lyrics led to its ban from radio stations and entirely in the state of Indiana. "On April 6, 1963, a bunch of dudes from Portland, Oregon spent 50 bucks to record a cover of an obscure 1957 R&B song called Louis Louis, originally done by a Louisiana singer named Richard Berry."

podcast.body: This version of the song was recorded for $50 in Portland, Oregon, on April 6, 1963, at Northwestern Motion Pictures and Recording. It was a bare-bones session with one microphone hung in the center of the room, forcing singer Joe Eli, who had just been fitted with heavy braces, to sing upward with difficulty. The band had only one take, leading to a rushed performance with visible errors including the drummer dropping a stick and Joe Eli coming in two bars too early. "The best example is Louis Louis by the Kingsman, a song recorded for $50 in Portland, Oregon, on April 6, 1963."
